name: Southeastern Ixtlán Zapotec
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 8. Zapotec accent falls on the last or second last syllable of the word. Tone is bound up with accent, affecting the accented syllable and the one following it, if there is one. Our material on tone is restricted to Ixtlan and Tehuantepec, and there has hardly been sufficient study even of these two. [...] Modern Ixtlan has four different tones on accented final syllables: low, high, rising, falling. On accented penults, there are only three: low, high, falling. The syllable following an accented penult is either low or high, but the high never follows the falling. There are thus five patterns: low-low, high-low, falling-low, high-high, low-high.
new_statements.citation: Swadesh, Morris. 1947. The phonemic structure of Proto-Zapotec. International Journal of American Linguistics 13(4): 220-230.
new_statements.locator: Section 8 'Accent and tone', p. 228 (IA scan, PDF page 24); informant/fieldwork note fn. 1, p. 220.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: is on file (16.4 MB, IA microfilm scan of IJAL 13(4) with text layer; open archive.org download listed). extracted text of PDF p. 24 gives journal p. 228, running head 'INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF AMERICAN LINGUISTICS VOL. XIII', and contains both halves of the quoted passage word for word: left column '8. Zapotec accent falls on the last or second last syllable of the word. Tone is bound up with accent, affecting the accented syllable and the one following it, if there is one. Our material on tone is restricted to Ixtlan and Tehuantepec, and there has hardly been sufficient study even of these two.' and right column 'Modern Ixtlan has four different tones on accented final syllabl…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (stress) in Ixtlan Zapotec lies within a two-syllable window at the right edge: on the final or the penultimate syllable, not predictable from Swadesh's statement (historically it stays on the original root syllable; when syllables were lost a penultimate accent was re-placed so the word is still penult-accented). Tone contrasts are licensed by the accented syllable (4 tones if final, 3 if penult) plus a reduced high/low contrast on the one post-tonic syllable; in compounds the first member loses its accent and tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent shift in Ixtlan 'evidently only when an old falling tone was involved' (kud 'dough'); in longer (compound) words the prior element loses accent and tone and the result remains penult-accented (Ix. 'water', 'heart', 'cotton' examples). Rising and falling tones never occur before glottal stop.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in citation forms (comparative wordlist of nouns/numerals); tone described as dependent on the accented syllable. Statement is framed for 'Zapotec' generally but the tone/accent data are explicitly Swadesh's own Ixtlan (and Tehuantepec) recordings.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement rests on Swadesh's own 1941 recordings from a speaker of the town of Ixtlan de Juarez ('Perez of Ixtlan'), which he takes as representative of the 'Sierra de Juarez' division. Ethnologue 15 (2005) lists Ixtlan de Juarez among the towns of zpd Southeastern Ixtlan Zapotec (center Santa Maria Yavesia; also Lachatao, Latuvi, San Miguel Amatlan, Capulalpan, Xiacui, Guelatao), WALS maps de Angulo & Freeland's 'Zapotec (Ixtlan)' [zpi] to zpd/sout3005, and Glottolog files the companion Swadesh 1949 chapter under sout3005 -- so the attribution to sout3005 follows the databases. Caveat: 'Ixtlan Zapoteco' is also an Ethnologue alternate name for zaa Sierra de Juarez (Atepec) Zapotec (glottocode sier1250), and de Angulo & Freeland's 'sub-dialect of Ixtlan' pools zpd towns (Lachatao, Llavesia=Yavesia) with zaa towns (Macuiltianguis, Ixtepeji, Xaltianguis). No description specific to Yavesia/Lachatao/Latuvi speech was found. Swadesh's sentence is phrased for Zapotec generally, with the tone-by-accent-position detail explicitly for 'Modern Ixtlan'.

sources.locator: Section 8 'Accent and tone', p. 228 (IA scan, PDF page 24); informant/fieldwork note fn. 1, p. 220.
sources.note: Sec. 8 'Accent and tone', p. 228: 'Zapotec accent falls on the last or second last syllable of the word. Tone is bound up with accent, affecting the accented syllable and the one following it'; Modern Ixtlan has four tones on accented final syllables (low, high, rising, falling), three on accented penults (low, high, falling), post-tonic syllable low or high; accent 'has evidently stayed for the most part in its original location', with shifts where syllables were lost; in compounds the accent and tone of the prior element are lost.

sources.citation: de Angulo, Jaime & L. S. Freeland. 1933-35. The Zapotekan linguistic group: a comparative study of Chinanteco, Chocho, Mazateco, Cuicateco, Mixteco, Chatino, and especially of Zapoteco proper and its dialects. Part I. IJAL 8(1): 1-38.
sources.note: Has a 'Sub-dialect of Ixtlan' (el idioma serrano) section with records from Ixtlan, Ixtepexi, Lachatao, Llavesia (=Yavesia), Los Arroyos, Macuiltianguis, Xaltianguis (pronouns/morphology only). General phonology pp. 4-6: 'The two outstanding features of the Zapotekan system are pitch tone and nasality'; footnote treats pitch, quantity, stress as part of the 'phonema'. No statement of where word stress falls in Zapoteco; the only explicit stress remark is about Chinanteco ('when tone and quantity are present, stress is absent'). Sole source behind WALS lect zpi 'Zapotec (Ixtlan)' = zpd.
